statements.quote: We collected each participant’s research proposal created prior to the study as part of their PhD application and marked it with reference to the criteria detailed in the appendix 3.
The dialogue exchanges were audio-recorded and then transcribed into textual form. Following this, dialogue transcripts were coded and analysed to unveil dynamics of verbal exchanges.
We used a customised questionnaire aimed to gauge learners’ perceptions. See Appendix 1 for the full questionnaire.
We randomly selected 18 students from the experimental groups to interview. The interview outlines consisted of 10 questions, referring to Appendix 2.

We asked both groups of students to submit a new research proposal based on the discussions undertaken with either Dou Bao or a peer. The proposal was then rated based on a marking scale, provided in Appendix 3.
Detailed descriptions and examples of the coding dimensions are shown in Table 1.
statements.locator: p. 10, Measures, Coding instrument for dialogue dynamics; Table 1 is on p. 11

statements.quote: The questionnaire was adapted from Venkatesh and Davis (2000) as well as Sun et al. (2024).
The complete questionnaire can be found in Appendix 1.
We adopted content analysis to evaluate the students’ research proposals based on the assessment criteria shown in Appendix 3.
statements.locator: p. 12, Measures of students’ practical competencies in CPS

statements.quote: Research proposals were anonymised prior to marker evaluation, to avoid marker bias. Two independent markers evaluated each research proposal independently. Marking criteria and model research proposals were provided to the independent markers prior to evaluation.
statements.locator: p. 12, Measures of students’ practical competencies in CPS

statements.quote: Two trained researchers coded the transcripts of the 80 exchanges (40 student-peer dialogue + 40 student-chatbot dialogue) simultaneously.

The analysis was conducted using GSEQ software, which calculates the Z-value by dividing the raw residuals (the difference between the observed and expected counts) by an estimate of the standard error (García-Farina et al., 2018).
Consequently, we constructed network graphs using Gephi software to visualise the significant sequences of the two interaction types, each consisting of a set of vertices and edges.
Additionally, all interview records were transcribed and analyzed using thematic analysis techniques (Braun & Clarke, 2006).
We did not use of AI tools to analyze and draw insights from data as part of the research process.

deposits.notes: Secondary systematic-review dataset deposited by Akbar Bahari and Yao Bin, titled 'From interaction with generative AI to human communication: A mixed-methods systematic review of communicative competence claims, measures, and transfer evidence in higher education' (published 2026-07-25; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21559413). It is not an original-data deposit by Song et al. The landing page and https://zenodo.org/api/records/21559413 both returned HTTP 200. The API listed all four files with the sizes recorded here. The XLSX file was downloaded in memory from https://zenodo.org/api/records/21559413/files/GenAI_CommComp_FULLTEXT_AUTHORITATIVE_FINAL.xlsx/content (HTTP 200; 157886 bytes), and all 15 worksheets were read. rows_checked and columns_checked describe OUTCOME_EFFECT_LEVEL: 71 rows across the review, not 71 participants. STUDY_LEVEL contains 39 rows; its ST037 row matches c165 by DOI 10.1186/s41239-025-00508-2 and Source_File s41239-025-00508-2.pdf. The same row incorrectly calls the authors 'Wang et al. (2025)', so it is treated only as a secondary extraction, not as authoritative evidence about the original trial. Four of the 71 outcome rows belong to ST037: EF065 (prior knowledge dialogue), EF066 (subjective dialogue), EF067 (elaboration dialogue), and EF068 (perceived usefulness). There is no row for the S1-O1 research-proposal total score. The group means, SDs, counts and calculated effects are study-level summaries; no participant ID, individual treatment assignment, individual outcome score, proposal text or participant dialogue transcript is present in the inspected workbook. has_outcome_scores=false means no individual outcome scores, despite aggregate score summaries. The Full_Text_Evidence_Excerpt column contains article text, not participants' texts or ideas. The RELIABILITY_UNITS and SPSS_RELIABILITY_EXPORT sheets each contain 624 review-coding rows, not trial participants. The three SAV files were listed but not read; their names correspond to study, effect and review-reliability exports. All worksheet row counts: README_FINAL=8; REVIEW_LOGIC=5; SOURCE_MANIFEST=39; STUDY_LEVEL=39; OUTCOME_EFFECT_LEVEL=71; RELIABILITY_UNITS=624; SPSS_STUDY_EXPORT=39; SPSS_EFFECT_EXPORT=71; SPSS_RELIABILITY_EXPORT=624; VARIABLE_CODEBOOK=28; VALUE_LABELS=119; SPSS_CROSSWALK_FINAL=63; VALIDATION_LOG=11; NON_POOLING_RULES=6; DESCRIPTIVE_SUMMARY=45.

notes:
The only located public data concerning S1 are a later review's aggregate extraction. No public participant-level dataset or output-level dataset with participant IDs was confirmed. 'public_partial' reflects that aggregate public deposit, not public access to the original study records. The original paper explicitly says, 'The data is available upon reasonable request.' No access request was made.

The entire 105544-character markdown conversion was read in six consecutive chunks, including the Appendix and references, covering the 30-page version of record. Key data/materials passages and appendix captions were checked against PDF text on pp. 9-10, 12-13 and 25-27. No repository, code-release, preregistration or separate supplementary-file link is named in the paper; both form data_and_code URL fields are empty. The Appendix publishes the perception questionnaire (Table 8), interview outline (Table 9) and proposal rubric (Table 10); Table 1 gives the dialogue coding categories. These are embedded article materials, not a separate participant-data deposit. GSEQ and Gephi are named analysis software, without shared scripts. The article's CC BY 4.0 license is not treated as a license for unshared participant data.

None of the missing statistics in final.open_items can be recovered from the confirmed public deposit: separate originality/rubric scores, baseline means/SDs, verified proposal-analysis counts and missing cases, raw versus adjusted proposal means, scoring aggregation, or uncertainty accounting for peer dependence remain unresolved. There are no participant proposals or dialogue transcripts for computing diversity. Published aggregate figures and the later reviewers' inferred/computed quantities do not establish original analysis counts or fill the missing participant data. Procedural questions about randomization, final-writing AI access, pairing, and marker qualifications also remain unresolved.

All network requests used Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 and no requester email address, authentication token, or account identifier. No web search engine, login, account creation, access request, CAPTCHA solution or bot-check bypass was used. API search counts are recorded as returned; failed requests use null. The initial Zenodo searches with size=100 returned HTTP 400; subsequent requests without that parameter succeeded. Broad name searches were not fully exhausted, and the publisher landing page was blocked by a Client Challenge despite HTTP 200; these limit confidence in the absence of additional deposits. The DOI resolver request https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00508-2 returned HTTP 200 Crossref JSON through content negotiation, with the matching title and first-author ORCID 0000-0001-5761-5477; it did not supply supplementary data. The first-author ORCID was used only as a public search key. A second Zenodo author-search hit, Fanyin, was excluded after its API metadata confirmed an unrelated historical-literature article. Repository file metadata and the inspected XLSX were held in memory; only this JSON report was written.

For completeness, all 71 distinct external HTTP(S) hyperlinks embedded in the PDF were requested once. These are article-license, author-identifier and bibliographic links, not original-study data repositories.
